section_summary: This section contains U.S. State Department diplomatic correspondence and reports concerning Japan's foreign relations and domestic affairs in late 1934 and early 1935. It comprises the concluding portion of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly political report for October 1934 (with lists of despatches and telegrams sent), a Far Eastern Affairs Division memorandum summarizing the November report, and Embassy Despatch No. 1083 transmitting the November 1934 monthly report. Primary subjects include the preliminary London naval conversations and Japan's move to terminate the Washington Naval Treaty, international friction over petroleum legislation and monopolies in Japan and Manchukuo, negotiations regarding the Chinese Eastern Railway, Kwantung Army administrative control, and political maneuvering surrounding the Okada Cabinet, the budget, and agrarian distress.

subfiles.about: The Tokyo Embassy's comprehensive monthly report reviewing Japanese foreign relations, domestic politics, and economic developments during October 1934, along with monthly lists of despatches and telegrams sent.
subfiles.from: Embassy of the United States of America, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This subfile contains pages 5 through 38 of the Tokyo Embassy's October 1934 monthly report, together with lists of despatches and telegrams sent to the Department during October. It details American-Japanese affairs, including the Kaiun Maru incident in the Philippines, anti-Japanese friction in Arizona's Salt River Valley, controversies surrounding the Japanese Petroleum Industry Law and the proposed Manchukuo oil monopoly, and preliminary naval conversations in London. It also reviews the British industrial mission under Lord Barnby, the Dutch-Japanese trade parley in Batavia, the 15th International Red Cross Conference in Tokyo, negotiations with the USSR over the Chinese Eastern Railway, and the administrative reorganization in Manchuria subordinating civil police to the Kwantung Army. Domestic sections cover cabinet tensions, a controversial War Office pamphlet advocating state socialism, agrarian problems, the 1935–36 budget, and legal proceedings against reactionary conspirators.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan during October 1934 (Monthly Political Report No. 97)

subfiles.about: A State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing key highlights of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for November 1934.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State (William T. Turner)
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by a transmittal sheet routed to and noted by the Under Secretary on January 16, 1935, this three-page memorandum provides an executive summary of Tokyo's political report for November 1934. It highlights Japanese press satisfaction with U.S. Democratic election victories, the decelerating negotiations over the Chinese Eastern Railway, and planned revisions to Soviet-Japanese fishery agreements. It also reviews tariff changes in Manchukuo penalizing American imports, the French refusal to join Japan in a common denunciation of the Washington Naval Treaty, Army leadership shifts placing General Minami in command of the Kwantung Army, and the proliferation of foreign trade barriers against Japanese commerce.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum: Tokyo's Monthly Political Report for November, 1934

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmitting Embassy Report No. 98 covering Japanese domestic and international conditions during November 1934.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Transmits Embassy Report No. 98 on conditions in Japan during November 1934. The report examines diplomatic tensions with the United States and Great Britain regarding the promulgation of the Manchukuo Petroleum Monopoly Law and enforcement of the Japanese Petroleum Industry Law, as well as the refused extradition of the Kaiun Maru crew. It reviews protracted negotiations for the sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway, border disputes with the USSR, the creation of an Anglo-Japanese Trade Council, and discussions with France and Great Britain concerning the London naval talks and Japan's intended abrogation of the Washington Naval Treaty. Domestically, the report records the appointment of veteran statesman Korekiyo Takahashi as Finance Minister following Sadanobu Fujii's resignation, life sentences handed down to Blood Brotherhood assassins, and debates in the extraordinary session of the Diet over rural relief and military budgets.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1083 Transmitting Report on Conditions in Japan during November 1934 (Report No. 98)
